UK Compulsory Liquidation Statistics

In April 2026 there were 371 compulsory liquidations in England and Wales, 18% of all company insolvencies. A compulsory liquidation is a court-ordered winding-up of a company, normally after a creditor presents a winding-up petition. HMRC is one of the most active petitioners. This page tracks the monthly trend back to 2000, the rate per 10,000 companies and how the procedure sits within the wider insolvency total.

Trend

Monthly UK compulsory liquidations since 2000

Because they require a court order, compulsory liquidations lag the economic cycle and track how actively creditors are pursuing debts. Volumes rose as HMRC resumed active enforcement after the pandemic.

View range

How to read this

What the compulsory liquidation figures show

Compulsory liquidations follow legal action, so they reflect creditor and HMRC enforcement as much as underlying trading conditions.

The count is a volume, not a failure rate. The rate per 10,000 companies adjusts for the size of the active register.

The leading indicator for compulsory liquidations is winding-up petition statistics. See also the UK company insolvency statistics and CVL statistics.

Method

UK company insolvency statistics: methodology

Company insolvency data is sourced mainly from Companies House. Compulsory liquidation data for England and Wales comes from the Insolvency Service, and compulsory liquidation data for Northern Ireland comes from the Department for the Economy in Northern Ireland.

The headline England and Wales figures use seasonally adjusted data where the Insolvency Service has identified seasonality. Scotland and Northern Ireland figures are shown on an unadjusted basis.

The statistics count formal company insolvency procedures. They do not include members' voluntary liquidations, dissolutions or ordinary company closures.

Data limitations

  • The latest month is provisional and can be revised.
  • Sector data is published one month behind the headline figures.
  • Industry is based on self-reported SIC codes.
  • Registered office addresses are not a reliable guide to where a company traded.
  • Solvent company closures are not included.
